candidates.title: Using an AI Agent Makes You a Sucker for Phishing Emails
candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s not exactly a challenge most of the time to identify a sketchy phishing email that crudely impersonates an otherwise trusted institution or tries to lure you into a too-good-to-be-true deal in a bid to steal your identity. However, your AI agent may not be quite as discerning. As cybersecurity software company Malwarebytes warns in a new post , AI assistants may fall prey to prompt injection attacks, a type of malicious message in which hackers — or possibly rogue AI agents — include hidden instructions designed to influence the victim’s AI. These instructions are frequently made unreadable by humans by concealing the nefarious text, “while leaving content available for an AI system to process,” Malwarebytes explains. To solve the problem, we can’t simply ask “people to look more carefully at their emails.” Instead, companies must carefully determine how AI assistants crawl through the data and extra relevant information from emails. “The real flaw is that the model can’t tell the difference between text it’s supposed to read and instructions it’s supposed to follow,” AI code review service ShipItClean developer Apollo Raines told Malwarebytes. “Stripping hidden content before it reaches the model is worth doing, and every vendor should do it.” As a result, people who are already wary of suspicious emails should learn to “distrust their AI assistant” as well, according to Raines. We’ve known about AI models’ vulnerability to prompt injection attacks for years now. But thanks to the advent of popular AI assistant tools like Meta’s Muse, that risk could be carried to its natural conclusion by having autonomous agents complete a string of tasks without any human supervision. It’s a flaw researchers have already encountered in AI-powered browsers , which — perhaps thankfully — have yet to gain any real traction. candidates.title: Scientists Puzzled as James Webb Detects Signal From Completely Empty Void in Space
candidates.raw_excerpt: Using the NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope, a team of researchers led by University of Minnesota astrophysicist Mason Huberty had a closer look at a group of almost 10,000 galaxies spanning billions of light-years in the Fornax constellation. As detailed in a new paper published in The Astrophysical Journal , they honed in on a small space in the region that they thought was entirely unoccupied. But to their astonishment, they observed a single emission line emanating from it — twice over a span of just three months. Emission lines are bright, narrow bands of light emitted at a specific wavelength by distant celestial objects and other phenomena. Puzzlingly, prior observations from the same region didn’t feature the same reading. Put simply, the JWST stared into the abyss — and the abyss stared back. Instead of hunting down already known objects, Huberty and his colleagues tried to use the James Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph to uncover new ones, as Science Alert explains . The team examined what they thought was an empty region twice, in August and November 2023, at different angles to rule out any artifacts. Out of seven total detections of emissions in the region, one stood out because they couldn’t match it to a distant galaxy. It also stood out as the only near-infrared emission without any other accompanying emission lines near it. It should’ve also shown up in earlier James Webb observations since it’s technically bright enough — but didn’t. The astronomers offered several possible explanations, none of which “provide a fully satisfactory explanation,” according to their paper. The emission line may have been produced by a galaxy dating back to the earliest days of the Universe. It could’ve also come from a younger galaxy or a supernova, both of which are usually accompanied by other emission lines. candidates.title: The Orionid meteor shower peaks next week! Here's what to expect
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, triggering a spectacular display of shooting stars as Earth plunges through the densest part of the debris trail shed by Halley's Comet. Here's what you need to know. When is the best time to see Orionid shooting stars? Orionid meteors are best spotted between the hours of midnight and dawn on Oct. 22, when 10-20 shooting stars may be seen brightening the night sky each hour under ideal dark-sky. The glare cast by the 74%-lit waxing gibbous moon will hide fainter shooting stars for much of the night. Thankfully, the lunar disk will set a few hours after midnight, leaving a window of beautifully dark sky before dawn in which to enjoy the full majesty of the annual meteor shower. Remember to use a trusted website like Time and Date to discover the exact moment of moonset for your location. Where should I look to see Orionid meteors? Orionid shooting stars will appear to originate from a patch of sky, or radiant, located close to the red giant star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion , which glistens above the southeastern horizon for stargazers in the U.S. during the early hours of Oct. 22. For the best views look 40-90 degrees away from the radiant, where the glowing trains left in the wake of the fast-moving meteors will be at their longest. Be sure to head away from artificial lights and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to fully adapt to the dark for the best What causes the Orionid meteor shower? The Orionid meteor shower is active each year as Earth passes through the stream of debris left behind by Comet 1P/Halley , which was observed by a fleet of spacecraft when it last visited the inner solar system in 1986. Shooting stars become visible when particles of the ancient comet collide with our planet's atmosphere at 147,600 miles per hour (237,539 kilometers per hour), vaporizing in a spectacular display of natural fireworks. candidates.title: Ancient warmth helped flowering plants dominate Earth, study finds
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Extreme global warmth drove both mass extinctions and explosions in plant diversity during two periods over the past 140 million years, offering new insights into how flowering plants became dominant on Earth, a new study has found.

The study examined fossilized pollen and spores to show that the mid-Cretaceous and early Cenozoic periods of extreme global warmth were central to plant evolution, both for flowering plants and the other main types on Earth, according to a statement released on Thursday by Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).

Researchers said that land plants sustain almost all terrestrial animals, fungi and bacteria, while flowering plants are the most productive and diverse group, with about 400,000 species worldwide.

The team examined more than 60,000 fossil occurrences and applied methods that overcome the major biases in the fossil record, generating revised estimates of fossil pollen and spore diversity over the past 130 million years, according to the study published in Nature Plants.

Both plant extinctions and the emergence of new but evolutionarily related plant groups occurred mostly during the two periods of extreme global warmth, said the study's co-author, UTAS Professor Greg Jordan.

Each interval lasted several million years, with warming simultaneously destroying and promoting plant diversity "over million-year timescales," Jordan said. In contrast, cooler periods were marked by little change in plant diversity.

However, the researchers warned that human-driven warming is likely to cause plant extinctions much faster than past extreme warming events.

candidates.title: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn , with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017 . Running low on fuel, NASA chose to steer Cassini straight into Saturn's atmosphere, where the spacecraft was destroyed . NASA's Cassini spacecraft lifts off on Oct. 15, 1997, atop a Titan IVB rocket. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered NASA's Cassini mission to Saturn (which carried the European Space Agency's Huygens lander to Titan) was a flagship planetary mission like no other ever when it first launched toward the ringed planet. The $3.26 billion Cassini spacecraft became the first probe ever to orbit Saturn when it arrived in 2004. It revealed Saturn's rings as active and dynamic structures, as intricate and complex as they are beautiful to observe. And it delivered Huygens to Titan, then followed up with a series of Titan flybys that revealed the cloudy moon could have liquid hydrocarbon rain, rivers, lakes and seas. Perhaps the most exciting discoveries were the most surprising. Cassini discovered a strange hexagon-shaped jetstream encircling Saturn's north pole and revealed massive hurricane-like vortexes over both of the planet's poles. In 2010, Cassini watched as a giant storm formed in Saturn's northern hemisphere, then grew to encircle the entire planet through 2011.
